content: Spider angioma, also known as spider naevus, is a benign and painless vascular malformation of the skin. It arises due to vasodilatory effects caused by various metabolic and hormonal disturbances. These lesions appear as small, blanchable red papules with radiating capillaries and are most commonly found on the face, arms, and trunk. While they can occur as solitary lesions without an underlying cause, multiple or extensive lesions often indicate an underlying etiology. Spider angiomas are frequently observed in patients with liver cirrhosis (e.g., due to alcoholism or viral hepatitis) or hyperestrogenic states (e.g., pregnancy or oral contraceptive use). Treatment primarily involves addressing the underlying cause, though facial lesions may be cauterized for cosmetic purposes. Spider angioma was first described by Dr. Erasmus Wilson, an English surgeon, in 1842 in his book on skin diseases. Later, in 1959, Dr. William Bennett Bean provided a detailed description of the lesion in his book on vascular spiders and related skin conditions. Spider angiomas can be classified into two groups: solitary vascular malformations without underlying conditions and multiple vascular malformations secondary to liver cirrhosis or hormonal imbalances. Dermoscopic classification includes network, looping, and star patterns. The pathophysiology of spider angiomas involves arteriolar vasodilation mediated by factors such as alcohol, substance P, hyperestrogenism, and impaired hepatic metabolism of steroid hormones. Studies in cirrhotic patients have shown a higher estradiol/testosterone ratio, suggesting that relative estrogen excess contributes to vasodilation and lesion formation. Mutations in the endoglin (ENG) and activin-receptor-like kinase (ALK1) genes, associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, have also been linked to increased spider angiomas. Common causes of spider angiomas include liver cirrhosis, hyperestrogenism, and thyrotoxicosis. Differential diagnoses include angiomata serpiginosum, basal cell carcinoma, cherry hemangioma, insect bites, and unilateral nevoid telangiectasia. The prevalence of spider angiomas is approximately 10,000–15,000 per 100,000 individuals in healthy adults and children worldwide. In children without liver involvement, 38% have at least one lesion, while 80% of children with cirrhosis have at least one lesion. The prevalence increases with age. Studies report a prevalence of 22% in normal male children and 30% in normal female children. About 33% of patients with advanced liver cirrhosis have spider angiomas. In pregnant women, spider angiomas are observed in approximately 53% of cases. They are more common in women of childbearing age, likely due to hyperestrogenic states. There is no documented gender predilection for spider angiomas in otherwise healthy populations. However, they are more common in pregnant women due to hyperestrogenic states. There is no racial predilection, but the lesions are more visible in light-skinned individuals. Risk factors include hyperestrogenic states (e.g., pregnancy, oral contraceptive use) and liver cirrhosis (e.g., due to alcohol or viral hepatitis). Patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia may have a higher number of angiomas. Most healthy children and adults with spider angiomas remain asymptomatic. Complications include bleeding secondary to manipulation and, in rare cases, relapsing gastrointestinal bleeding in those with internal lesions. The prognosis is excellent with resolution of the underlying cause. Physiological spider angiomas in younger adults often increase until puberty and then disappear with age. Lesions that develop during pregnancy may resolve postpartum, and those associated with oral contraceptive use may resolve after discontinuation of the hormonal preparation. There are no specific diagnostic criteria for spider angiomas. When not extensive, they are benign. Extensive lesions may indicate an underlying cause, such as alcoholism or hyperestrogenic states. Physical examination reveals a central red spot with radiating thin-walled vessels and surrounding erythema. Unusually large lesions with visible pulsatile blood flow have been reported. Spider angiomas are typically found on the face, chest, and arms in the distribution of the superior vena cava, though unusual presentations in the eyelids, pleura, esophagus, and gastrointestinal tract have been documented. Diascopy, a procedure involving pressure application with a glass slide or paper, is used to assess blanchability. Pallor upon pressure application, followed by refilling upon pressure release, is characteristic of spider angiomas. Laboratory workup should include liver function tests, viral markers, pregnancy tests, estrogen and FSH levels, and thyroid function tests (T3, T4, TSH) to identify potential underlying causes. There are no specific findings on ECG, X-ray, echocardiography, or ultrasound directly associated with spider angiomas. However, ultrasound and CT scans are useful for identifying underlying liver cirrhosis or ovarian tumors. Biopsy may be helpful in atypical presentations and can reveal diagnostic features such as a cutaneous arterial net, central spider arteriole, subepidermal ampulla, and star-shaped efferent vessels. Treatment is generally unnecessary as spider angiomas cause no imminent harm. Cosmetic treatment options include fine-needle electrocautery, 595 nm pulse-dye laser (PDL), 532 nm KTP laser, or electro-desiccation, which have been used successfully with minimal scarring. Addressing the underlying cause, such as improving hepatic function or discontinuing agents causing hyperestrogenic states, often leads to resolution of the lesions. There are no primary preventive measures for spider angiomas.
